summary: Earth’s surface is in an endless dance of natural processes and human activities, but radar data that tracks these changes is hard to read for anyone outside science. SARbit is an interactive educational web app that makes data from NISAR (the NASA-Indian Space Research Organisation Synthetic Aperture Radar mission) accessible to amateur explorers and citizen scientists who want to learn what Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) can do. Through gamified missions at real 2026 events around the world (floods in Mozambique and Spain, deforestation in the Amazon, crop cycles in India and Israel, the shrinking Great Salt Lake and oil infrastructure in the Mississippi Delta), users compare before-and-after L-band radar images (24 cm wavelength) and combine two polarizations, HH (sent and received horizontally) and HV (sent horizontally, received vertically), into interactive change-detection maps to locate where the surface changed. Every answer is computed from the real radar echo values, and each mission explains the physical drivers behind the signal. A Radar Lab lets users experiment with thresholds, speckle and scattering. By showing how SAR sees through clouds and darkness, SARbit translates complex radar observations into insights about how surface changes impact ecosystems, water resources, agriculture and local communities.
details:
SARbit is an interactive educational web app that helps amateur explorers understand Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) through real data from NISAR (the NASA-Indian Space Research Organisation SAR mission). Users play an alien with a radar that sees through clouds and darkness, and explore seven real 2026 surface changes: floods in Mozambique and Spain, Amazon deforestation, crop cycles in India and Israel, the drying Great Salt Lake, and oil platforms in the Mississippi Delta.

How it works: In each mission users compare before-and-after L-band radar images, combine HH and HV polarizations (horizontal or vertical send and receive) into their own change-detection map, then locate the change. Answers are computed from the real radar values, and each mission explains the physical driver: calm floodwater reflects radar away, cleared forest loses canopy echo, metal platforms shine bright. A Radar Lab lets users experiment with thresholds, speckle and scattering.

Benefits and impact: No account, installation or prior knowledge needed. SARbit makes NISAR data accessible and links radar signals to impacts on ecosystems, water resources, agriculture and communities. Anyone can add their own study area with one script.

Tools: NISAR GCOV data from NASA ASF DAAC; Python, GDAL and FME for processing; JavaScript and Leaflet for the web app; Vercel hosting; NASA GIBS optical imagery; OpenStreetMap.

Creativity: Each event has its own game: a platform treasure hunt, lassoing clearings, a rice-season timeline. “Radar glasses” make polarization tangible.

Factors considered: Scientific honesty (same orbit geometry only, no thresholds low enough to turn radar noise into fake change), physical interpretation (HH revealed the most change, likely from L-band double bounce off trunks and stems; dry salt flats and water both look dark), accessibility for any device, and future NISAR applications such as ground-motion maps of volcanoes, earthquakes and Dead Sea sinkholes.
